hero.heading: Anything a machine can check, a human should never have to check.
hero.subtitle: Backend architecture for Java and the Spring ecosystem, with boundaries your build defends. Once a decision lives in the structure, the agreed way becomes the only way.
decide.heading: Make it impossible, make it visible or leave it to judgment.
decide.intro: Every rule gets exactly one of these three levels. The work lies in deciding which.
decide.1.title: Make it impossible
decide.1.body: Data integrity, access, legal requirements. A double-booked resource or a publication without a translation must never be able to exist in the first place. Rules like these go into constraints and publishing gates.
decide.2.title: Make it visible
decide.2.body: Violations that fail a check and can be overridden with a reason. An architecture test that turns red forces a decision, not a standstill.
decide.3.title: Leave it to judgment
decide.3.body: No check can decide whether content that does not come from a template is right. What is not deterministic stays with people, as do design questions that only know trade-offs.
decide.position: Conventions that only live in a wiki do not exist. There are rules built into the system and well-documented wishes. A standard whose violation does not break a build is a request.
decide.position.support: I have watched well-documented decisions get ignored in practice often enough.
decide.diagram.aria: Spectrum from hard-enforced through made visible to human judgment, with rule types as dots: data integrity, access rights and legal requirements are hard-enforced, layer rules, naming conventions and deprecations are made visible, design trade-offs and content without a template stay with judgment
hero.visual.aria: Diagram: a modulith made of six domains with two hexagonal modules each: sales with catalogue and pricing, ordering with cart and orders, finance with invoices and payments, logistics with inventory and shipping, customers with accounts and messaging, service with returns and complaints. Inside each domain the two modules are directly connected and consume no events from each other: high cohesion inside, low coupling outside. Outward, every module hangs on the horizontal event bus without exception, through two lines each, one publishing, one subscribing. An access from inventory straight into invoices, past the bus, is stopped at the module boundary
pattern.heading.status_quo: Does any of this sound familiar?
pattern.1.title: Discipline Dependency
pattern.1.reality: Conventions and knowledge live in people's heads. They work as long as someone is watching or maintaining them.
pattern.3.title: Decisions Without Effect
pattern.3.reality: Decisions were agreed on and documented on paper or in wikis, but nowhere did they get enforced consistently.
pattern.5.title: Workarounds as the Norm
pattern.5.reality: What started as an exception is now a new norm.
pattern.7.title: Generated Code Ignores Your Wiki
pattern.7.reality: When generated code meets conventions that only exist as documentation, they most likely get ignored. Like someone with too much on their plate: they take the shortcut. As long as nobody checks, everything counts, and as long as no error surfaces, nothing happens.
schema.service.description: Curfee designs backend software architecture for Java and the Spring ecosystem, for existing systems as well as new designs, delivered as project-based engagements rather than hourly services. Architecture decisions are anchored in the system, through architecture tests such as ArchUnit and CI gates, so violating them is either visible or impossible. No feature code is written: the only code in the client repo is the architecture tests that hold the designed boundaries. Available across Austria, Germany, and Switzerland (DACH region).
scope.heading: What I do and what I don't.
scope.intro: I design backend architecture for Java and the Spring ecosystem: the cut into modules, the domain model with its invariants, the transaction boundaries, the integration with the outside. Whether a modulith is enough or separate services are needed, I decide by what operations can carry and which boundaries have proven themselves. Every decision is anchored as an architecture test in your CI, a violation breaks the build.

about.heading: I am Philipp Höllinger.
engagements.heading: Selected engagements
engagements.1.title: Double-booking a courtroom became impossible.
engagements.1.body: A court booking system enabled the very errors it was meant to prevent: double-booked courtrooms, past-dated bookings, unchecked conflicts. I designed the rebuild and built integrity into every layer, from validation rules to conditional checks inside the transaction.
engagements.1.diagram.aria: Example: a conflicting booking hits a conditional check inside the transaction and is refused with an error
engagements.1.diagram.label: Refused booking
engagements.1.diagram.comment: Conditional check: does the booking overlap?
engagements.2.title: A summer job became a single click.
engagements.2.body: For years, five students spent each summer reading organiser emails and typing every event into the system by hand. I designed the flow around self-service: organisers submit their own listings and an automated import loads them daily. All that remains is to check the content, adjust a detail where needed, and click publish.
engagements.2.diagram.aria: Diagram: organisers fill a self-service event form, entries import daily, one click publishes them
engagements.2.diagram.form.title: Submit your event
engagements.3.title: Every publication became bilingual.
engagements.3.body: The EU Single Digital Gateway required administrative information to be structured, multilingual, and machine-readable, yet no system could produce it. I designed the publishing system around predefined fields and a required translation step: editors fill the fields in German, and nothing goes live until the English translation exists. Metadata and publication run on their own.
engagements.3.diagram.aria: Diagram: editors fill predefined fields in German, a page can only go public once the English translation exists
engagements.3.diagram.form.title: Predefined fields
engagements.4.title: An architecture violation becomes a failing build.
engagements.4.body: The pipeline checks layer rules and dependency directions. A PR that violates the architecture concept cannot merge. Reviewers stop policing conventions and review what machines cannot judge: design intent and tradeoffs.
engagements.4.diagram.aria: Diagram: a pull request check list where build and tests pass, the architecture check fails, and the merge is blocked
engagements.4.diagram.title: Pull request checks
about.who.logistics: I started by coordinating workflows between goods, employees, and processes. When people with different approaches work together, structure matters more than discipline.
about.who.stack: I have worked with Java and Spring for more than five years.
about.who.quote: What drives me is an obsession with the things that go unnoticed, the small details that shape the future of an environment.
about.who.why.3: Before I change anything, I want to understand how it affects an organisation and the people working with it. The most common mistake I have seen is the opposite: systems and the workflows between them, implemented first and understood later.
about.who.why.2: I am a minimalist and call myself an advocate of simple concepts. They outlast any sophisticated process that runs on discipline and quietly breaks over time. And small changes that keep paying off over time create as much value as one big fix for one big pain.

privacy.personal: Personal data is collected only to the extent technically necessary, with purpose limitation and data minimisation applied throughout. Collected data is never disclosed to third parties without a legal basis. Three legal grounds may apply. Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR) covers cases where you have given consent for one or more specific purposes. Performance of a contract (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR) covers cases where processing is needed to perform a contract you are party to, or to take steps at your request before entering into one. Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR) covers cases where processing is necessary for legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, unless those interests are overridden by your fundamental rights and freedoms.
privacy.rights.heading: Rights of data subjects
privacy.rights: As a data subject, you have the following rights. Access (Art. 15 GDPR): confirmation whether your personal data is being processed, along with information about such data and its processing. Rectification (Art. 16 GDPR): correction of inaccurate or incomplete personal data. Erasure (Art. 17 GDPR): deletion of your personal data, subject to the conditions laid down in Art. 17. Restriction of processing (Art. 18 GDPR): limits on how your personal data is processed. Data portability (Art. 20 GDPR): a copy of your personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. Objection (Art. 21 GDPR): the right to object at any time, on grounds relating to your particular situation, to processing of your personal data.

collab.heading: First the assessment, then we build.
collab.body: The assessment takes a few weeks. After that we design and build, in months, not years. Scope and duration are agreed up front. Every rule built in has an owner and a cheap change path. The details belong in the first conversation.
faq.heading: Questions you might have.
faq.1.question: How is this different from classic enterprise architecture?
faq.1.answer: Classic enterprise architecture produces target pictures for slides and governance for boards. I start from the reality of your system landscape, and with your team we build decisions into your systems: the ones already made, and the ones still to be made.
faq.2.question: We are not on Spring. Are you still an option?
faq.2.answer: For design and consulting, yes. How a system is cut and which patterns hold does not depend on Spring. I do not develop code outside Java and Spring.
faq.3.question: How much of your team's time does this take?
faq.3.answer: The assessment takes 30 to 60 minutes per person. During the embedding we build the checks in the hours your team already spends on the system. Nobody is pulled onto a project on the side.
faq.4.question: What happens if you become unavailable or the mandate ends?
faq.4.answer: Nothing that waits for a deadline. Every rule is built in as soon as it is decided, and runs in your systems from then on. There is no big bang at the end: if the mandate ends or I am unavailable, everything already built in stays in operation.
faq.5.question: Why an individual and not an agency?
faq.5.answer: Agencies usually have an incentive to sell developer hours. As an individual I do not. My work is about designing something, simplifying it and getting it to the point, not about selling extra hours.
